title: Spent 2 weeks building a tool instead of my game.. Zero regret.
author: Dream_Ep
selftext:
You know that moment when you procrastinate on your game by building a tool you "need"?

Yeah. That was me for the past 2 weeks.

So I'm glad to introduce my full workflow to generate sprite sheet for game !

So it's a 100% free AI workflow to generate game sprites fast (no paid tools, no manual frame-by-frame) thanks to my 2 in one tools for sprite sheet generator.

Workflow:

1. Nano Banana → Base sprite
Generate a clean pixel-art character. Keep prompts simple and consistent.

2. Grok → Animations
Create short looping videos (idle / run / death). Think in video loops, not frames.

3. SpriteMaster – AI Video → Sprite Sheet
 - Extract frames at custom FPS
 - Auto-crop + smart centering
 - Chroma key background removal
 - Halo cleanup for clean transparency
 - Export PNG sheet / GIF / ZIP
(Runs 100% client-side, files stay local)
SpriteMaster – Sheet Manager
 - Merge multiple animations, auto-detect grids, reorganize frames, resize, and export a final ready-to-use sheet.

Why I use this pipeline:

- 100% free
- Browser-based
- Very fast iteration
- Works directly for Unity / Godot / Unreal

Full AI workflow breakdown here: https://spritemaster.pages.dev/

PS: If you have any recommendations or feedback please don't hesitate, I will try to launch my website on product hunt tomorrow 🎉

comments.author: Dream_Ep
comments.body:
Hey everyone, quick update!  
  
I wanted to show the actual result of my workflow in action since some of you look skeptical.

I generated 3 separate AI animations for the same character (thanks to Grok Imagine in my case)  — walk, dash, and death — then ran each through SpriteMaster to extract the frames, remove backgrounds, clean up halos, and resize to 64x64 pixel art. The key is to be consistent for your video generation of each character animation, you should have a base prompt for you character and then quickly add details of the animation you want.  
  
The key thing here is consistency across animations. Because you're working from AI-generated videos of the same character, you get matching style and proportions across all three sprite sheets. 

Here's the final result, by the way I'm just back home and make it in 2 min approximately : 

https://preview.redd.it/3r0uep1jaiig1.png?width=1024&format=png&auto=webp&s=25494d3ba3f76c2957d5162b77b8c059a346dad2

  
Then SpriteMaster's Sheet Manager lets you merge them into a single organized sheet.

u/AlpsTurbulent5404 — this is exactly the kind of workflow I had in mind. AI video → sprite sheet → game-ready assets,  all without touching Photoshop or manually cutting frames. The 64x64 format works great for pixel art games, and nearest-neighbor scaling keeps those hard edges crisp.

If anyone wants to try it:   
  
[https://spritemaster.pages.dev](https://spritemaster.pages.dev)   
  
— still 100% free, runs entirely in your browser.   
  
Please if you used the tool give me any feedback and upgrade you would like !

Also you have the possibility to chose from 3 distinct algorithm for the resizing part and chose the one which fit the most to your stylé.

replies.author: didwecheckthetires
replies.body:
It depends on the kind of game.  For pixel art, 64x64 is extremely big for top-down or side-scrolling 2D games.  The exception is fighting games, where the sprites can get huge and very, very expensive (like $100k per character).    
When you see larger sprites, it's usually because they're drawn smaller and scaled up.  Pixel art games are often built at 320x180, 480x270, or 640x360 then scaled to the monitor resolution. So the assets you see are displayed 3x-6x larger than they were drawn.

comments.author: FocusKontrol
comments.body: I did a similar “AI tool break” from my game. But I vibe coded an AI video editor. I had a problem that creating video content of my game took too much time away from development but you need to be constantly posting keep up a momentum on social media. So now instead of just joining together and editing clips, I annotate my gameplay clips with subtitles for AI to understand what’s going on when in all available clips. Now there’s a library of different clips AI can choose from. Now there’s workflow is: I give a very vague video idea like “Would you play this game? Combine various game mechanics clips together. In the end invite people to join discord”. The agent puts together a script and produces a video editor project file. It does automatic TTS and music, video descriptions etc. I used to make 1 video for like 1-2h. Now I make about 4-5 videos per hour and do all the videos for the week in less than half a work day.

replies.author: Dream_Ep
replies.body: Mate it looks so good, you did a very nice job. Is that possible to share your workflow / tool ?

replies.author: FocusKontrol
replies.body: I’m not quite willing to share a plug n play product, but the idea is simple to get started 1. Gather all your clips 2. Make subtitles for them using Subtitle edit (explain what’s happening and when) 3. Install Claude code with remotion and try explaining what video you want. I used kdenlive myself for some more advanced audio stuff, but I think remotion is more compatible with Claude code and you can get something started within a day. The main point is rethinking the philosophy of clip->edit->video  to instead clip->annotate-> use clip content in 100s of videos with different contexts with the help of AI.
